=== Caddyfile.prod ===
# The production host.
#
# NOTHING RUNS HERE YET. There is no production VPS, no production Supabase
# project and no production DNS record; this file is the role written ahead
# of the box, so that provisioning production later is running provision.sh
# with APIVO_HOST_ROLE=prod rather than designing a deployment under time
# pressure on the day it is first needed.
#
# It is deliberately the same file as Caddyfile.preprod with one site instead
# of two: production must not be the environment with its own bespoke proxy
# config that nothing has rehearsed. Staging exercises every line of this
# except the hostname.
{
	auto_https disable_redirects

	log {
		output stdout
		format json
	}
}

import /etc/caddy/snippets.caddy

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Production — final semver tags only (v0.2.0), behind an approval gate.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
https://{$APIVO_PROD_HOST} {
	import origin-tls origin
	import hardening
	import crawler-fence
	import apivo-routes apivo-prod-api apivo-prod-web
}

# The apex/www counterpart, whichever of the two production is not served on.
# Cloudflare can do this redirect at the edge instead; it is here so the
# origin is correct on its own, and so a Cloudflare rule that is deleted by
# accident degrades to a redirect rather than to a certificate error.
https://{$APIVO_PROD_ALT_HOST} {
	import origin-tls origin
	redir https://{$APIVO_PROD_HOST}{uri} permanent
}

:443 {
	tls internal
	abort
}

:80 {
	abort
}

=== snippets.caddy ===
# Shared Caddy snippets. Imported by Caddyfile.preprod and Caddyfile.prod so
# the routing rule and the response hardening are written once and cannot
# drift between environments.

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# (hardening) — what every response from every environment carries.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
(hardening) {
	encode zstd gzip

	header {
		# The deployment is https-only and says so. `preload` is deliberately
		# NOT among these: submitting a domain to the browser-vendor preload
		# list is a commitment that outlives the deployment, and it is not
		# reversible on any useful timescale.
		#
		# This mattered on Cloudflare only for a custom domain (workers.dev
		# sits under an HSTS-preloaded TLD). Here it matters on every
		# hostname: nothing upgrades a first plain-http visit for us.
		Strict-Transport-Security "max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains"

		# Caddy names itself in every response otherwise. The version of the
		# reverse proxy is not information a caller needs.
		-Server
	}
}

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# (crawler-fence) — FR-013, founder decision D6.
#
# The retired Worker refused declared crawlers at the edge, and it did so for
# a specific reason that survives the move: `/api/…` is routed AROUND the web
# container, and web/src/middleware.ts — the fence everything else relies on
# — ships inside that container. The Go api has no inbound User-Agent check.
# Without this block, `curl -H 'User-Agent: GPTBot' https://<host>/api/v1/front`
# returns the article corpus as JSON on every environment and every preview,
# where the Worker returned 403.
#
# Applied to the whole site, as the Worker did, so it covers the HTML pages
# too. That is deliberate duplication: D6 says the fence is never the sole
# enforcement, and the copy in the web container stays.
#
# `Vary: User-Agent` because the same URL answers differently by User-Agent
# and a shared cache must never hand one audience the other's response.
#
# THE LIST IS DUPLICATED — a third copy, alongside deploy/cloudflare/routing.js
# and web/src/middleware.ts. deploy/hetzner/validate.sh asserts this one and
# routing.js's agree, so the copies cannot drift silently. The way to get back
# to one copy is to move the fence into Go middleware on the api, next to the
# rate limiter that belongs there for the same reason.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
(crawler-fence) {
	@crawler header_regexp User-Agent (?i)(GPTBot|ClaudeBot|CCBot|Google-Extended|Bytespider|PerplexityBot|Amazonbot|meta-externalagent|ia_archiver|archive\.org_bot|Googlebot|Bingbot|DuckDuckBot|Baiduspider|YandexBot|Applebot)
	handle @crawler {
		header Vary User-Agent
		respond 403
	}
}

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# (apivo-routes) — which container answers.
#
# Replaces the path routing that deploy/cloudflare/routing.js did, with the
# same split: the API answers /api/…, /healthz and /readyz; the Astro
# frontend answers everything else. The API is not published on a host port
# in any environment and this is the only thing that talks to it.
#
# The Worker went to some length to decode the path once and collapse
# repeated slashes before testing it, because /api/v1/%65ditorial/queue is
# editorial to the Go router and looked like nothing in particular to a
# naive prefix test. That care was load-bearing for the Worker's RATE LIMIT,
# which was expressed as an inversion over paths — a path that slipped past
# the test went unlimited.
#
# It is not load-bearing here, and the difference is worth stating rather
# than leaving to be rediscovered. This snippet only chooses an upstream:
# every /api/… path lands on the Go router either way, and what an editorial
# route requires — a valid JWT, and the editor role enforced a second time
# by the database — is enforced in Go, by the same code, whatever proxy is
# in front. Caddy also matches on Go's already-decoded r.URL.Path, so the
# encoding trick above resolves before any matcher sees it.
#
# The rate limit itself has NOT moved here, and nothing else carries it: the
# Worker that used to is no longer deployed. There is currently NO rate limit
# on the editorial endpoints in this deployment. docs/ENVIRONMENTS.md names
# porting it to Go middleware as a precondition for anything being publicly
# reachable.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
(apivo-routes) {
	# /api/v1/*, not /api/*: the api serves nothing under /api/ but v1, and
	# the frontend serves endpoints of its own under /api/ - the retailer
	# page's click-out posts to /api/cashback/clickout, the guided tours
	# read /api/tour/*. A matcher on the whole prefix sent both to the api,
	# which answered 404, and a click-out that never reached the frontend
	# is a member sent nowhere (#546). validate.sh proves both halves.
	@api path /api/v1/* /healthz /readyz

	handle @api {
		reverse_proxy {args[0]}:8080
	}

	handle {
		# HTTPS to the frontend container, and the reason is Astro.url.
		#
		# @astrojs/node builds the request URL from the SOCKET and the Host
		# header (astro/dist/core/app/node.js):
		#
		#     const isEncrypted = 'encrypted' in req.socket && req.socket.encrypted;
		#     const protocol = isEncrypted ? 'https' : 'http';
		#
		# X-Forwarded-Proto is not consulted anywhere in that path, in
		# standalone or middleware mode. Over plain http the frontend
		# therefore believes it is on http://, and Astro's own CSRF
		# middleware compares that against the browser's https:// Origin
		# with === and refuses every form post the site makes of itself:
		# sign-in, approval, withdrawal, source registration.
		#
		# This used to be papered over here, by rewriting the browser's
		# Origin and Referer back to http:// before the container saw them.
		# That rewrite is gone, and good riddance:
		#
		#   - It needed the hostname at PARSE time, because `header_up` does
		#     not expand placeholders in its search argument. A wildcard
		#     preview host has no such name, so previews never had it and
		#     every editorial form there was refused.
		#   - It made the CSRF property depend on the proxy getting a
		#     find-and-replace exactly right, on three of them, forever.
		#
		# Giving the container a certificate makes the socket genuinely
		# encrypted, so Astro.url is genuinely https and the check works
		# unaided - here, on previews, and anywhere else this ever runs.
		#
		# The certificate is self-signed (provision.sh writes it per
		# environment) and deliberately not verified: the upstream is one
		# hop away on a private compose network, addressed by container
		# name. This encrypts the hop without claiming to have
		# authenticated it, which is the same trade the Postgres
		# connections make with sslmode=require.
		# TLS is asked for on the TRANSPORT, not by putting https:// in the
		# upstream address. Caddy refuses a placeholder in an address that
		# carries a scheme - "due to parsing difficulties, placeholders are
		# not allowed when an upstream address contains a scheme" - and the
		# preview snippet below has no choice but a placeholder, since its
		# container name is derived per request. The scheme form parses
		# here, where {args[1]} is substituted before the address is read,
		# and that difference is exactly the trap: one idiom that works in
		# both places is worth more than two that each work in one.
		#
		# It is the same shape of limitation that killed the Origin rewrite
		# this replaces. Caddy expands placeholders in a great many
		# positions and not in these, and neither refusal is visible until
		# something runs.
		reverse_proxy {args[1]}:4321 {
			transport http {
				tls
				tls_insecure_skip_verify
			}
		}
	}
}

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# (origin-tls) — the certificate Cloudflare's proxy connects to.
#
# A Cloudflare Origin Certificate: free, valid for years, trusted by
# Cloudflare and by nothing else, which is exactly right for a certificate
# that should only ever be presented to Cloudflare. Set the zone to
# "Full (strict)" so Cloudflare verifies it.
#
# provision.sh installs it. There is no ACME here on purpose: HTTP-01 through
# an orange-clouded record is unreliable, and DNS-01 would mean a Cloudflare
# API token with DNS edit rights sitting on the VPS — a much larger key than
# the one problem it solves. docs/ENVIRONMENTS.md records how to move to
# DNS-01 later if wildcard per-PR preview hostnames make it worth it.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
(origin-tls) {
	tls /etc/caddy/certs/{args[0]}.pem /etc/caddy/certs/{args[0]}.key
}

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# (apivo-preview-routes) — one open pull request, at pr-<n>.<preview domain>.
#
# Same split as (apivo-routes): the API answers /api/…, /healthz and /readyz,
# the frontend answers everything else. The upstream is derived from the
# hostname at request time, so a pull request opening does not require the
# proxy in front of QA and Staging to be restarted.
#
# {re.preview.1} is the `pr-<n>` captured by the @preview matcher in the site
# block that imports this. The caller does not get to choose it freely: that
# matcher admits only ^pr-[0-9]+ , so `apivo-qa-api.example.com` is refused
# rather than turned into a container name.
#
# It is a CAPTURE and not {labels.N} because a label index counts from the
# right, and so silently depends on how deep the preview domain is. See the
# long note in Caddyfile.preprod; the short version is that {labels.3} is
# correct for pr-1.qa.example.com and EMPTY for pr-1.example.com, and the
# difference is invisible to `caddy validate`.
#
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# WHAT A PREVIEW USED TO BE UNABLE TO DO
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
#
# There was no Origin/Referer rewrite here, and for a while that meant a
# preview's editorial FORM POSTS were refused while QA's identical ones
# worked. It was absent because it could not be made to work: `header_up`
# does not expand placeholders in its search argument, so the per-request
# hostname was unusable; the named environments passed their host as a
# parse-time snippet argument instead, and a WILDCARD site has no single
# host to pass. The regexp form (`re:` with a capture reference) does not
# substitute in Caddy 2.10 - tested against `$1`, `{re.1}` and
# `{http.regexp.<name>.1}`, all of which left the header untouched.
#
# It was written off as costing nothing, because a preview shipped with
# PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL empty and nobody could sign in to be refused. That
# reasoning expired the moment previews borrowed QA's auth project, and
# sign-in is itself a form post.
#
# The rewrite is now gone everywhere, and no site needs one. The frontend
# container is reached over TLS, so Astro.url carries the scheme the browser
# actually used, and BOTH origin checks agree with it unaided: Astro's own
# built-in one, which compares whole origins, and web/src/lib/csrf.ts, which
# compares hosts. The preview was the environment that could not be fixed by
# rewriting headers, which is how it came to be fixed properly.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
(apivo-preview-routes) {
	# /api/v1/* for the reason (apivo-routes) gives: the frontend has
	# endpoints of its own under /api/, and a preview that swallowed them
	# would not show a reviewer the click-out it was opened for.
	@preview-api path /api/v1/* /healthz /readyz

	handle @preview-api {
		reverse_proxy apivo-{re.preview.1}-api:8080
	}

	handle {
		# TLS for the same reason as (apivo-routes), and this is the site
		# that forced it: a wildcard host could never have had the Origin
		# rewrite, so a preview's sign-in was refused while QA's worked.
		reverse_proxy apivo-{re.preview.1}-web:4321 {
			transport http {
				tls
				tls_insecure_skip_verify
			}
		}
	}
}

	# the frontend serves endpoints of its own under /api/ - the retailer
	# page's click-out posts to /api/cashback/clickout, the guided tours
	# read /api/tour/*. A matcher on the whole prefix sent both to the api,
	# which answered 404, and a click-out that never reached the frontend
	# is a member sent nowhere (#546). validate.sh proves both halves.
	@api path /api/v1/* /healthz /readyz

	handle @api {
		reverse_proxy {args[0]}:8080
	}

	handle {
		# HTTPS to the frontend container, and the reason is Astro.url.
		#
		# @astrojs/node builds the request URL from the SOCKET and the Host
		# header (astro/dist/core/app/node.js):
		#
		#     const isEncrypted = 'encrypted' in req.socket && req.socket.encrypted;
		#     const protocol = isEncrypted ? 'https' : 'http';
		#
		# X-Forwarded-Proto is not consulted anywhere in that path, in
		# standalone or middleware mode. Over plain http the frontend
		# therefore believes it is on http://, and Astro's own CSRF
		# middleware compares that against the browser's https:// Origin
		# with === and refuses every form post the site makes of itself:
		# sign-in, approval, withdrawal, source registration.
		#
		# This used to be papered over here, by rewriting the browser's
		# Origin and Referer back to http:// before the container saw them.
		# That rewrite is gone, and good riddance:
		#
		#   - It needed the hostname at PARSE time, because `header_up` does
		#     not expand placeholders in its search argument. A wildcard
		#     preview host has no such name, so previews never had it and
		#     every editorial form there was refused.
		#   - It made the CSRF property depend on the proxy getting a
		#     find-and-replace exactly right, on three of them, forever.
		#
		# Giving the container a certificate makes the socket genuinely
		# encrypted, so Astro.url is genuinely https and the check works
		# unaided - here, on previews, and anywhere else this ever runs.
		#
		# The certificate is self-signed (provision.sh writes it per
		# environment) and deliberately not verified: the upstream is one
		# hop away on a private compose network, addressed by container
		# name. This encrypts the hop without claiming to have
		# authenticated it, which is the same trade the Postgres
		# connections make with sslmode=require.
		# TLS is asked for on the TRANSPORT, not by putting https:// in the
		# upstream address. Caddy refuses a placeholder in an address that
		# carries a scheme - "due to parsing difficulties, placeholders are
		# not allowed when an upstream address contains a scheme" - and the
		# preview snippet below has no choice but a placeholder, since its
		# container name is derived per request. The scheme form parses
		# here, where {args[1]} is substituted before the address is read,
		# and that difference is exactly the trap: one idiom that works in
		# both places is worth more than two that each work in one.
		#
		# It is the same shape of limitation that killed the Origin rewrite
		# this replaces. Caddy expands placeholders in a great many
		# positions and not in these, and neither refusal is visible until
		# something runs.
		reverse_proxy {args[1]}:4321 {
			transport http {
				tls
				tls_insecure_skip_verify
			}
		}
	}
}

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# (origin-tls) — the certificate Cloudflare's proxy connects to.
#
# A Cloudflare Origin Certificate: free, valid for years, trusted by
# Cloudflare and by nothing else, which is exactly right for a certificate
# that should only ever be presented to Cloudflare. Set the zone to
# "Full (strict)" so Cloudflare verifies it.
#
# provision.sh installs it. There is no ACME here on purpose: HTTP-01 through
# an orange-clouded record is unreliable, and DNS-01 would mean a Cloudflare
# API token with DNS edit rights sitting on the VPS — a much larger key than
# the one problem it solves. docs/ENVIRONMENTS.md records how to move to
# DNS-01 later if wildcard per-PR preview hostnames make it worth it.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
(origin-tls) {
	tls /etc/caddy/certs/{args[0]}.pem /etc/caddy/certs/{args[0]}.key
}

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# (apivo-preview-routes) — one open pull request, at pr-<n>.<preview domain>.
#
# Same split as (apivo-routes): the API answers /api/…, /healthz and /readyz,
# the frontend answers everything else. The upstream is derived from the
# hostname at request time, so a pull request opening does not require the
# proxy in front of QA and Staging to be restarted.
#
# {re.preview.1} is the `pr-<n>` captured by the @preview matcher in the site
# block that imports this. The caller does not get to choose it freely: that
# matcher admits only ^pr-[0-9]+ , so `apivo-qa-api.example.com` is refused
# rather than turned into a container name.
#
# It is a CAPTURE and not {labels.N} because a label index counts from the
# right, and so silently depends on how deep the preview domain is. See the
# long note in Caddyfile.preprod; the short version is that {labels.3} is
# correct for pr-1.qa.example.com and EMPTY for pr-1.example.com, and the
# difference is invisible to `caddy validate`.
#
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# WHAT A PREVIEW USED TO BE UNABLE TO DO
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
#
# There was no Origin/Referer rewrite here, and for a while that meant a
# preview's editorial FORM POSTS were refused while QA's identical ones
# worked. It was absent because it could not be made to work: `header_up`
# does not expand placeholders in its search argument, so the per-request
# hostname was unusable; the named environments passed their host as a
# parse-time snippet argument instead, and a WILDCARD site has no single
# host to pass. The regexp form (`re:` with a capture reference) does not
# substitute in Caddy 2.10 - tested against `$1`, `{re.1}` and
# `{http.regexp.<name>.1}`, all of which left the header untouched.
#
# It was written off as costing nothing, because a preview shipped with
# PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL empty and nobody could sign in to be refused. That
# reasoning expired the moment previews borrowed QA's auth project, and
# sign-in is itself a form post.
#
# The rewrite is now gone everywhere, and no site needs one. The frontend
# container is reached over TLS, so Astro.url carries the scheme the browser
# actually used, and BOTH origin checks agree with it unaided: Astro's own
# built-in one, which compares whole origins, and web/src/lib/csrf.ts, which
# compares hosts. The preview was the environment that could not be fixed by
# rewriting headers, which is how it came to be fixed properly.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
(apivo-preview-routes) {
	# /api/v1/* for the reason (apivo-routes) gives: the frontend has
	# endpoints of its own under /api/, and a preview that swallowed them
	# would not show a reviewer the click-out it was opened for.
	@preview-api path /api/v1/* /healthz /readyz

	handle @preview-api {
		reverse_proxy apivo-{re.preview.1}-api:8080
	}

	handle {
		# TLS for the same reason as (apivo-routes), and this is the site
		# that forced it: a wildcard host could never have had the Origin
		# rewrite, so a preview's sign-in was refused while QA's worked.
		reverse_proxy apivo-{re.preview.1}-web:4321 {
			transport http {
				tls
				tls_insecure_skip_verify
			}
		}
	}
}

# The pre-production host: QA and Staging, side by side on one VPS.
#
# Hostnames come from the environment so no domain is committed here —
# provision.sh writes them into /etc/apivo/edge/caddy.env. Caddy refuses to
# start on an unset {$VAR} in a site address rather than serving something
# nobody meant, which is the failure mode to want.
{
	# Every site below presents a certificate this file names explicitly (a
	# Cloudflare Origin Certificate — see the (origin-tls) snippet), so Caddy
	# never issues one and never needs an ACME account or an email. What is
	# switched off here is only the automatic :80 -> :443 redirect vhost:
	# Cloudflare terminates the browser's TLS and always reaches this origin
	# on 443, so a redirect listener would exist purely to be scanned.
	auto_https disable_redirects

	# Access logs as JSON on stdout, which the docker json-file driver
	# rotates (deploy/hetzner/compose/docker-compose.edge.yml). A VPS has a
	# finite disk and nothing sweeping it.
	log {
		output stdout
		format json
	}
}

import /etc/caddy/snippets.caddy

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# QA — every push to main lands here, automatically, within a minute.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
https://{$APIVO_QA_HOST} {
	import origin-tls origin
	import hardening
	import crawler-fence
	import apivo-routes apivo-qa-api apivo-qa-web
}

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Staging — release candidates only (v0.2.0-rc.1 and friends).
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
https://{$APIVO_STAGING_HOST} {
	import origin-tls origin-staging
	import hardening
	import crawler-fence
	import apivo-routes apivo-staging-api apivo-staging-web
}

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Previews — one per open pull request, at pr-<n>.{$APIVO_PREVIEW_DOMAIN}.
#
# The origin certificate must cover this wildcard, and it is the SAME
# certificate QA presents (`origin`) because previews live in the QA
# hostname's zone: Cloudflare includes the apex and the first-level wildcard
# in a zone's certificate by default, so one certificate per zone covers
# ra1ze.com and *.ra1ze.com together. Staging is a different zone and so a
# different certificate (`origin-staging`).
#
# Two certificates rather than one covering everything, because the
# Cloudflare DASHBOARD cannot issue a certificate spanning zones - only its
# API can. Requiring the API here would have put a curl and an Origin CA Key
# between a new host and its first byte served, to save copying one more
# file. This needs no ACME and no DNS API token on the host either way.
#
# The matcher is the security boundary: only ^pr-[0-9]+ reaches the routing
# snippet, so no other label can be turned into a container name to proxy at.
# Everything else on the wildcard is refused here rather than 502-ing
# somewhere further in.
#
# It matches on the HOST PREFIX rather than on a label index, and that is not
# a style preference. `{labels.N}` counts from the RIGHT, so the leftmost
# label of a preview host is {labels.3} only when the preview domain has
# exactly two labels. Point previews at a one-level domain — pr-1.example.com
# rather than pr-1.qa.example.com — and {labels.3} is the EMPTY STRING: the
# matcher never fires, every preview 403s, and the upstream degrades to
# `apivo--api`. Nothing warns, because the config is still valid.
#
# The suffix needs no checking here: Caddy's `*` matches exactly one label, so
# reaching this block already proves the host is <something>.<preview domain>
# (a.b.example.com does not match *.example.com at all). Asserting the prefix
# is therefore asserting the whole name.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
https://*.{$APIVO_PREVIEW_DOMAIN} {
	import origin-tls origin
	import hardening

	@preview header_regexp preview Host ^(pr-[0-9]+)\.
	handle @preview {
		import crawler-fence
		import apivo-preview-routes
	}

	handle {
		abort
	}
}

# Anything arriving on an address this file does not name is refused without
# naming what does live here. In practice that is a scan straight at the VPS
# IP: Cloudflare only ever sends the two hostnames above, and the firewall
# provision.sh installs only admits Cloudflare's ranges in the first place.
# This is the third layer, not the first.
:443 {
	tls internal
	abort
}

:80 {
	abort
}

content.content:
1	#!/bin/sh
2	# The deploy. One environment, one tick.
3	#
4	# Usage: apivo-reconcile <env>
5	#
6	# Nothing pushes to this host. No CI job holds an SSH key, no agent has a
7	# shell here, and there is no inbound webhook to forge: the host decides,
8	# every minute, whether what it is running is what its channel says it should
9	# be, and converges if it is not. That is the whole deployment mechanism.
10	#
11	# A systemd timer runs this per environment (apivo-reconcile@qa.timer). It is
12	# also the manual deploy command - `systemctl start apivo-reconcile@qa` - so
13	# the path a person takes in a hurry is the same path that runs unattended,
14	# and is therefore as tested as the automatic one.
15	#
16	#   1. read the environment's channel tag (qa | staging | prod)
17	#   2. resolve it to an image DIGEST at the registry, without pulling
18	#   3. if the digest is what is already running, converge and stop
19	#   4. otherwise: pin the digest, roll out, and PROVE the roll-forward
20	#   5. if the proof fails, put the previous digest back
21	#
22	# The distinction in (2) is the point of the whole design: a tag is what an
23	# environment TRACKS, a digest is what it RUNS. Every container on every
24	# environment is pinned by digest, so "what is running in staging" has one
25	# answer that cannot drift under a tag someone moved.
26	#
27	# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
28	# Exit codes
29	#   0  converged (whether or not anything changed)
30	#   1  a rollout failed; the previous digest was restored, or could not be
31	#   2  usage or configuration error - nothing was attempted
32	# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
33	#
34	# Everything the script touches outside itself goes through a variable, so
35	# the test suite can substitute a stub and prove the decisions without a
36	# registry, a daemon, or a container:
37	#
38	#   APIVO_DOCKER   the docker command                 (default: docker)
39	#   APIVO_ETC      per-environment configuration      (default: /etc/apivo)
40	#   APIVO_STATE    what is running, and what was      (default: /var/lib/apivo)
41	set -eu
42	
43	DOCKER="${APIVO_DOCKER:-docker}"
44	ETC="${APIVO_ETC:-/etc/apivo}"
45	STATE="${APIVO_STATE:-/var/lib/apivo}"
46	
47	# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
48	# Logging: one JSON object per line, on stdout, for journald to capture.
49	#
50	# JSON rather than prose because this is the log an agent reads to answer
51	# "what happened to my deploy" without a shell on the box - the same reason
52	# the api emits JSON at APP_ENV=prod. `msg` is the only field that can carry
53	# arbitrary text, so it is the only one escaped.
54	# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
55	log() {
56	    _level="$1"
57	    _event="$2"
58	    _msg="$3"
59	    _msg=$(printf '%s' "$_msg" | sed -e 's/\\/\\\\/g' -e 's/"/\\"/g' | tr -d '\n\r\t')
60	    printf '{"level":"%s","event":"%s","env":"%s","msg":"%s"}\n' \
61	        "$_level" "$_event" "${ENV_NAME:-?}" "$_msg"
62	}
63	
64	die() {
65	    log error "${1}" "${2}"
66	    # ::error:: as well as the JSON line: this script is also run by hand and
67	    # from CI, where the annotation is what a person actually sees.
68	    #
69	    # FLATTENED, because the message can now carry a subprocess's own output
70	    # - buildx's, on a failed resolve - and that output is multi-line. A
71	    # workflow command is line-oriented: a newline mid-message ends the
72	    # annotation early, spills the rest as loose log lines, and a line
73	    # beginning `::error::` inside that remainder would be an annotation
74	    # nobody wrote. Removing the newlines closes both at once.
75	    #
76	    # Newlines become SPACES rather than being deleted, unlike log(): that
77	    # writes a JSON string for tooling, where a lost space costs nothing,
78	    # while this line is read by a person and `read-only file systemERROR:`
79	    # is a worse sentence than the one buildx wrote.
80	    #
81	    # `::` itself is deliberately left alone. It is only a workflow command
82	    # at the START of a line, which the flattening already prevents, and
83	    # escaping it would corrupt any IPv6 address that appears in an error -
84	    # a registry failure is exactly where one shows up.
85	    _annotation=$(printf '%s' "${2}" | tr '\n\r\t' '   ')
86	    echo "::error::apivo-reconcile ${ENV_NAME:-?}: ${_annotation}" >&2
87	    exit "${3:-1}"
88	}
89	
90	if [ "$#" -ne 1 ]; then
91	    echo "usage: $0 <env>" >&2
92	    exit 2
93	fi
94	
95	ENV_NAME="$1"
96	# The environment name becomes container names, network names and file paths.
97	# It arrives from a systemd unit instance, which is user-supplied text, so it
98	# is validated rather than trusted: anything outside this set could escape a
99	# path or name a container in another environment.
100	case "$ENV_NAME" in
101	'' | *[!a-z0-9-]*)
102	    die usage "environment name '$ENV_NAME' is not lowercase alphanumeric with dashes" 2
103	    ;;
104	esac
105	
106	ENV_DIR="$ETC/$ENV_NAME"
107	STATE_DIR="$STATE/$ENV_NAME"
108	STACK_ENV="$ENV_DIR/stack.env"
109	
110	[ -r "$STACK_ENV" ] || die config "no readable $STACK_ENV; this host does not serve the '$ENV_NAME' environment (provision.sh creates it)" 2
111	
112	# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
113	# The maintenance switch. A reconciler with no way to stop it is a reconciler
114	# that fights an operator who is mid-investigation: `docker compose stop` on a
115	# broken container would be undone within the minute, along with the evidence.
116	# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
117	if [ -e "$ENV_DIR/paused" ]; then
118	    log info paused "reconciliation is paused by $ENV_DIR/paused; remove it to resume"
119	    exit 0
120	fi
121	
122	# stack.env is structural configuration only - no application secrets - so
123	# sourcing it into this shell is deliberate and bounded. DATABASE_URL and the
124	# translation credential live in api.env, which the Docker daemon reads
125	# directly as the service's env_file and this script never opens.
126	set -a
127	# shellcheck source=/dev/null
128	. "$STACK_ENV"
129	set +a
130	
131	# How long to wait for every container to report healthy before calling the
132	# rollout failed. The api migrates the schema on boot, so this is not just
133	# process start-up; a long migration on a large table is the case that makes
134	# a short timeout roll back a deploy that would have come up fine.
135	#
136	# Resolved AFTER stack.env is sourced, because stack.env is the only place
137	# docs/RELEASING.md tells an operator to set it and this unit has no
138	# EnvironmentFile. Read before the source, the value an operator wrote would
139	# be silently ignored and a long migration would be rolled back at 180s for
140	# reasons the journal never mentions.
141	WAIT_TIMEOUT="${APIVO_WAIT_TIMEOUT:-180}"
142	
143	for _required in APIVO_ENV APIVO_CHANNEL APIVO_REGISTRY COMPOSE_FILE; do
144	    eval "_value=\${$_required:-}"
145	    [ -n "$_value" ] || die config "$STACK_ENV does not set $_required" 2
146	done
147	
148	[ "$APIVO_ENV" = "$ENV_NAME" ] || die config "$STACK_ENV sets APIVO_ENV=$APIVO_ENV but this unit is '$ENV_NAME'; the two name the same environment or neither is trustworthy" 2
149	# The frontend's certificate, checked HERE rather than left to the container.
150	#
151	# compose sets SERVER_CERT_PATH and SERVER_KEY_PATH, which is what makes
152	# @astrojs/node serve https - and therefore what makes Astro.url carry the
153	# scheme the browser used, without which the site refuses its own form posts.
154	# Its standalone entry reads both files at startup with a plain readFileSync.
155	#
156	# Absent, that throws ENOENT and the container dies, restarts, and dies
157	# again. Nothing anywhere says why: a bind mount whose source is missing is
158	# CREATED EMPTY by Docker rather than refused, so the mount looks fine, the
159	# stack looks like it is merely unhealthy, and the actual sentence -
160	# "no such file or directory, open '/run/web-certs/web.crt'" - is buried in
161	# a restarting container's log.
162	#
163	# A host provisioned before this existed has no such file, so this is the
164	# state an upgrade lands in. It is worth one stat and a sentence that names
165	# the fix.
166	WEB_CERTS="$ENV_DIR/web-certs"
167	if [ ! -r "$WEB_CERTS/web.crt" ] || [ ! -r "$WEB_CERTS/web.key" ]; then
168	    die config "no frontend certificate at $WEB_CERTS; the web container would crash-loop on startup rather than serve. Re-run provision.sh on this host - it is idempotent and writes one per environment." 2
169	fi
170	
171	
172	API_REPO="$APIVO_REGISTRY/api"
173	WEB_REPO="$APIVO_REGISTRY/web"
174	
175	mkdir -p "$STATE_DIR"
176	CURRENT="$STATE_DIR/current"
177	PREVIOUS="$STATE_DIR/previous"
178	IMAGES_ENV="$STATE_DIR/images.env"
179	
180	# The digests the last successful rollout pinned, loaded before ANY compose
181	# invocation.
182	#
183	# This has to happen here rather than only inside the rollout, because the
184	# quiet path runs `compose up -d` too - that is what makes the reconciler
185	# self-healing - and the compose files declare
186	# `image: ${APIVO_API_IMAGE:?...}`. Without these in the environment, the most
187	# frequently executed path in the whole system fails on every tick with an
188	# unset variable, and reports a degraded environment that is in fact running
189	# perfectly well.
190	#
191	# Absent on a host that has never rolled out. That is not an error: the
192	# rollout below is what creates the file, and every path that runs compose
193	# before then sets these itself.
194	if [ -r "$IMAGES_ENV" ]; then
195	    set -a
196	    # shellcheck source=/dev/null
197	    . "$IMAGES_ENV"
198	    set +a
199	fi
200	
201	# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
202	# Resolve a tag to the digest the registry serves for it, WITHOUT pulling.
203	#
204	# `buildx imagetools inspect` is a registry query: on the overwhelmingly
205	# common tick - nothing has changed - this is two HTTP requests and no image
206	# data crosses the wire. Pulling first and comparing afterwards would work
207	# too, and would move gigabytes a day for an answer that is almost always
208	# "no".
209	# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
210	resolve_digest() {
211	    # `{{println .Manifest.Digest}}`, NOT `{{.Manifest.Digest}}`.
212	    #
213	    # buildx ignores a --format that BEGINS with `{{.Manifest` and prints its
214	    # human-readable block instead - verified against buildx v0.31.1, the
215	    # version get.docker.com installs:
216	    #
217	    #   --format '{{.Manifest.Digest}}'         -> Name: ...\nMediaType: ...\nDigest: ...
218	    #   --format 'X{{.Manifest.Digest}}Y'       -> Xsha256:afa5c8...Y
219	    #   --format '{{println .Manifest.Digest}}' -> sha256:afa5c8...
220	    #
221	    # The trigger is purely the leading token, so the obvious form is the one
222	    # that silently does not work. It returns a multi-line block with exit 0,
223	    # which passes the emptiness check below, never matches a recorded digest,
224	    # and ends as `docker pull repo@Name:  ...` - rejected as an invalid
225	    # reference, reported as a registry failure, and no environment ever rolls
226	    # forward on any host.
227	    #
228	    # The error is KEPT, not sent to /dev/null. Discarding it cost an
229	    # afternoon on the first host ever provisioned: buildx said
230	    # `mkdir /root/.docker/buildx: read-only file system` and the operator
231	    # saw only "cannot resolve", whose three suggested causes were all wrong.
232	    # A `docker pull` by hand worked, which made the registry and the
233	    # credential look fine and left nothing to go on.
234	    #
235	    # It comes back on STDOUT, merged, rather than in a variable the caller
236	    # reads afterwards: this runs inside a command substitution, so a
237	    # variable set here dies with the subshell and the caller would print
238	    # nothing (or, under `set -u`, abort with a shell error instead of the
239	    # diagnosis). The exit status says which kind of output this is.
240	    $DOCKER buildx imagetools inspect "$1" --format '{{println .Manifest.Digest}}' 2>&1
241	}
242	
243	# The one line of that output that is actually a digest.
244	#
245	# Anchored, so the human-readable block buildx prints when it ignores the
246	# --format (`Digest:    sha256:...`, with leading text) does NOT match and is
247	# correctly treated as "no digest". It also means a warning on stderr cannot
248	# be mistaken for the answer now that stderr is merged in.
249	digest_line() {
250	    printf '%s\n' "$1" | sed -n 's/^\(sha256:[0-9a-f][0-9a-f]*\)$/\1/p' | head -n 1
251	}
252	
253	read_state_field() {
254	    # read_state_field <file> <key> - absent file or key yields empty, which
255	    # every caller treats as "nothing is recorded", never as an error.
256	    [ -r "$1" ] || return 0
257	    sed -n "s/^$2=//p" "$1" | head -n 1
258	}
259	
260	compose() {
261	    # COMPOSE_FILE is exported from stack.env, so docker compose finds its own
262	    # files; the project name comes from the `name:` key in the base file.
263	    $DOCKER compose "$@"
264	}
265	
266	# What the environment should be running, according to its channel. A failure
267	# reports buildx's own words rather than a guess at what went wrong.
268	if ! API_OUT=$(resolve_digest "$API_REPO:$APIVO_CHANNEL"); then
269	    die registry "cannot resolve $API_REPO:$APIVO_CHANNEL - $API_OUT. Nothing was changed; the environment keeps serving whatever it already had. If a plain 'docker pull' of that reference works by hand but this does not, the difference is the systemd sandbox this unit runs under, not the registry or the credential." 1
270	fi
271	if ! WEB_OUT=$(resolve_digest "$WEB_REPO:$APIVO_CHANNEL"); then
272	    die registry "cannot resolve $WEB_REPO:$APIVO_CHANNEL - $WEB_OUT. Nothing was changed; the environment keeps serving whatever it already had. If a plain 'docker pull' of that reference works by hand but this does not, the difference is the systemd sandbox this unit runs under, not the registry or the credential." 1
273	fi
274	API_DIGEST=$(digest_line "$API_OUT")
275	WEB_DIGEST=$(digest_line "$WEB_OUT")
276	
277	if [ -z "$API_DIGEST" ] || [ -z "$WEB_DIGEST" ]; then
278	    die registry "cannot resolve $APIVO_REGISTRY/{api,web}:$APIVO_CHANNEL - buildx exited 0 but printed no digest, which is either a channel the publish workflow has never moved or the --format trap documented on resolve_digest. Nothing was changed; the environment keeps serving whatever it already had." 1
279	fi
280	
281	RUNNING_API=$(read_state_field "$CURRENT" API_DIGEST)
282	RUNNING_WEB=$(read_state_field "$CURRENT" WEB_DIGEST)
283	
284	# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
285	# The quiet path: the channel has not moved.
286	#
287	# `up -d` still runs, without --wait, and that is the self-healing property
288	# rather than a redundant call: a container that died, was OOM-killed, or was
289	# stopped by hand comes back on the next tick. It is a no-op when everything
290	# is already running, and it is the reason there is no separate "is anything
291	# down" alarm to write.
292	# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
293	if [ -n "$RUNNING_API" ] && [ "$API_DIGEST" = "$RUNNING_API" ] && [ "$WEB_DIGEST" = "$RUNNING_WEB" ]; then
294	    if compose up -d --remove-orphans >/dev/null 2>&1; then
295	        exit 0
296	    fi
297	    die converge "the channel has not moved, but bringing the existing stack up failed; the environment may be degraded. Check: docker compose ps" 1
298	fi
299	
300	log info rollout_start "$APIVO_CHANNEL moved: api ${RUNNING_API:-none} -> $API_DIGEST, web ${RUNNING_WEB:-none} -> $WEB_DIGEST"
301	
302	# The digests are pulled before anything is torn down, so a registry that
303	# fails half way costs nothing: the running stack is untouched until every
304	# byte of the new one is on the host.
305	if ! $DOCKER pull -q "$API_REPO@$API_DIGEST" >/dev/null 2>&1 || ! $DOCKER pull -q "$WEB_REPO@$WEB_DIGEST" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
306	    die registry "failed to pull the pinned digests; the running stack was not touched" 1
307	fi
308	
309	# The version the release pipeline stamped into the image, read from the
310	# image itself rather than from the tag that led here. This is what the
311	# frontend renders in its footer and what the release probe compares against,
312	# so it must come from the artefact.
313	image_version() {
314	    _v=$($DOCKER image inspect --format '{{index .Config.Labels "org.opencontainers.image.version"}}' "$1" 2>/dev/null || true)
315	    [ -n "$_v" ] || _v=dev
316	    printf '%s' "$_v"
317	}
318	
319	IMAGE_VERSION=$(image_version "$API_REPO@$API_DIGEST")
320	WEB_VERSION=$(image_version "$WEB_REPO@$WEB_DIGEST")
321	
322	# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
323	# The two channel tags do not move atomically.
324	#
325	# publish.yml points api:<channel> and web:<channel> at their digests in two
326	# separate registry calls, and this host may tick between them. Resolving the
327	# tags independently would then pin a NEW api beside the PREVIOUS web, roll it
328	# out, and report success - because the only version assertion downstream is
329	# against the api. A frontend a release behind its API is exactly the state
330	# that produces a blank page or a 500 on a field the old template does not
331	# know about.
332	#
333	# Refusing here costs nothing: the channel has not been consumed, so the next
334	# tick sixty seconds later sees the matched pair and rolls it out. The only
335	# way this becomes permanent is if the publish itself half-failed, which is a
336	# real problem that should be loud rather than silently deployed.
337	# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
338	if [ "$IMAGE_VERSION" != "$WEB_VERSION" ]; then
339	    log info version_skew "api is $IMAGE_VERSION but web is $WEB_VERSION; waiting for the channel to settle"
340	    exit 0
341	fi
342	
343	write_images_env() {
344	    # write_images_env <api-digest> <web-digest> <version>
345	    # Written whole to a temporary file and renamed, so a compose run that
346	    # starts mid-write can never read half a pin. Same directory, so the
347	    # rename stays within one filesystem and cannot degrade to copy-then-
348	    # delete.
349	    _tmp="$IMAGES_ENV.new"
350	    {
351	        echo "# Written by apivo-reconcile. Hand edits are overwritten on the next tick."
352	        echo "APIVO_API_IMAGE=$API_REPO@$1"
353	        echo "APIVO_WEB_IMAGE=$WEB_REPO@$2"
354	        echo "APIVO_VERSION=$3"
355	    } > "$_tmp"
356	    mv "$_tmp" "$IMAGES_ENV"
357	    set -a
358	    # shellcheck source=/dev/null
359	    . "$IMAGES_ENV"
360	    set +a
361	}
362	
363	record_state() {
364	    # record_state <file> <api-digest> <web-digest> <version>
365	    _tmp="$1.new"
366	    {
367	        echo "API_DIGEST=$2"
368	        echo "WEB_DIGEST=$3"
369	        echo "VERSION=$4"
370	        echo "AT=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)"
371	    } > "$_tmp"
372	    mv "$_tmp" "$1"
373	}
374	
375	# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
376	# Prove the roll-forward.
377	#
378	# `up -d --wait` returning 0 means every container reported HEALTHY, by its
379	# own healthcheck, which for the api means the binary answered its own
380	# /healthz. That is necessary and not sufficient: the PREVIOUS container
381	# answers a healthcheck just as happily if the new one never replaced it.
382	#
383	# So the containers are asked which image they are actually running, and it
384	# must be the digest just pinned. On Cloudflare this question could only be
385	# answered by trusting an HTTP response; here the daemon knows, so the
386	# stronger check is also the cheaper one.
387	# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
388	verify_running_digest() {
389	    # verify_running_digest <container> <expected-ref>
390	    _got=$($DOCKER container inspect --format '{{.Config.Image}}' "$1" 2>/dev/null || true)
391	    [ "$_got" = "$2" ] && return 0
392	    log error digest_mismatch "$1 is running '${_got:-nothing}', not the pinned '$2'"
393	    return 1
394	}
395	
396	# And then, end to end: the frontend container fetches the api's /healthz
397	# across the compose network and reports the version the api SERVES. It
398	# proves the network path, the api's readiness and the version stamp in one
399	# request, and it needs no extra image on the host - the frontend runs Node,
400	# whose built-in fetch is what its own healthcheck already uses.
401	served_version() {
402	    $DOCKER exec "apivo-$ENV_NAME-web" node -e \
403	        'fetch("http://apivo-'"$ENV_NAME"'-api:8080/healthz").then(r=>r.json()).then(j=>process.stdout.write(String(j.version||""))).catch(()=>process.exit(1))' \
404	        2>/dev/null || true
405	}
406	
407	roll_out() {
408	    # roll_out <api-digest> <web-digest> <version>
409	    write_images_env "$1" "$2" "$3"
410	    compose up -d --remove-orphans --wait --wait-timeout "$WAIT_TIMEOUT" || return 1
411	    verify_running_digest "apivo-$ENV_NAME-api" "$API_REPO@$1" || return 1
412	    verify_running_digest "apivo-$ENV_NAME-web" "$WEB_REPO@$2" || return 1
413	
414	    _served=$(served_version)
415	    if [ "$_served" != "$3" ]; then
416	        log error version_mismatch "the api serves version '${_served:-no answer}', expected '$3'"
417	        return 1
418	    fi
419	    return 0
420	}
421	
422	if roll_out "$API_DIGEST" "$WEB_DIGEST" "$IMAGE_VERSION"; then
423	    # The state that was good is kept as the rollback target only AFTER the
424	    # new one is proven, so `previous` always names a rollout that once
425	    # served rather than merely one that was attempted.
426	    [ -r "$CURRENT" ] && cp "$CURRENT" "$PREVIOUS"
427	    record_state "$CURRENT" "$API_DIGEST" "$WEB_DIGEST" "$IMAGE_VERSION"
428	
429	    # Yesterday's images are the other way a small host fills its disk.
430	    #
431	    # The age filter is load-bearing, not caution. Every image here is pulled
432	    # BY DIGEST, so none of them carries a tag - and an untagged image is
433	    # what `docker image prune` calls dangling and removes by default. The
434	    # release this host would roll back to is untagged and, once the new one
435	    # is serving, referenced by no container: a bare prune is entitled to
436	    # delete the very thing `previous` names. `apivoctl rollback` would then
437	    # depend on re-pulling from a registry that may be exactly what is
438	    # unavailable when someone is breaking glass.
439	    #
440	    # `until` keeps anything pulled in the last week, which covers every
441	    # rollback target worth having while still bounding the disk.
442	    $DOCKER image prune -f --filter "until=${APIVO_IMAGE_RETENTION:-168h}" >/dev/null 2>&1 || true
443	
444	    log info rollout_ok "$ENV_NAME now serves $IMAGE_VERSION (api $API_DIGEST)"
445	    exit 0
446	fi
447	
448	# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
449	# The rollout failed. Put back what was serving.
450	# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
451	log error rollout_failed "rolling back $ENV_NAME to the previous digest"
452	
453	PREV_API=$(read_state_field "$CURRENT" API_DIGEST)
454	PREV_WEB=$(read_state_field "$CURRENT" WEB_DIGEST)
455	PREV_VERSION=$(read_state_field "$CURRENT" VERSION)
456	
457	if [ -z "$PREV_API" ]; then
458	    die rollback_impossible "the rollout failed and there is no previous digest to return to - this environment has never had a successful one. It is DOWN. The channel still points at the broken build, so every tick will retry it: pause with 'touch $ENV_DIR/paused' before investigating, and check 'docker compose logs'." 1
459	fi
460	
461	if roll_out "$PREV_API" "$PREV_WEB" "${PREV_VERSION:-dev}"; then
462	    die rolled_back "the rollout failed and $ENV_NAME was rolled back to ${PREV_VERSION:-the previous digest}. The channel still points at the broken build, so the next tick will try it again - fix it forward, or move the channel back." 1
463	fi
464	
465	die rollback_failed "the rollout failed AND the rollback to ${PREV_VERSION:-the previous digest} also failed. $ENV_NAME is DOWN and no automatic path remains: pause with 'touch $ENV_DIR/paused', then investigate with 'docker compose ps' and 'docker compose logs'." 1
466

#!/bin/sh
# The deploy. One environment, one tick.
#
# Usage: apivo-reconcile <env>
#
# Nothing pushes to this host. No CI job holds an SSH key, no agent has a
# shell here, and there is no inbound webhook to forge: the host decides,
# every minute, whether what it is running is what its channel says it should
# be, and converges if it is not. That is the whole deployment mechanism.
#
# A systemd timer runs this per environment (apivo-reconcile@qa.timer). It is
# also the manual deploy command - `systemctl start apivo-reconcile@qa` - so
# the path a person takes in a hurry is the same path that runs unattended,
# and is therefore as tested as the automatic one.
#
#   1. read the environment's channel tag (qa | staging | prod)
#   2. resolve it to an image DIGEST at the registry, without pulling
#   3. if the digest is what is already running, converge and stop
#   4. otherwise: pin the digest, roll out, and PROVE the roll-forward
#   5. if the proof fails, put the previous digest back
#
# The distinction in (2) is the point of the whole design: a tag is what an
# environment TRACKS, a digest is what it RUNS. Every container on every
# environment is pinned by digest, so "what is running in staging" has one
# answer that cannot drift under a tag someone moved.
#
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Exit codes
#   0  converged (whether or not anything changed)
#   1  a rollout failed; the previous digest was restored, or could not be
#   2  usage or configuration error - nothing was attempted
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
#
# Everything the script touches outside itself goes through a variable, so
# the test suite can substitute a stub and prove the decisions without a
# registry, a daemon, or a container:
#
#   APIVO_DOCKER   the docker command                 (default: docker)
#   APIVO_ETC      per-environment configuration      (default: /etc/apivo)
#   APIVO_STATE    what is running, and what was      (default: /var/lib/apivo)
set -eu

DOCKER="${APIVO_DOCKER:-docker}"
ETC="${APIVO_ETC:-/etc/apivo}"
STATE="${APIVO_STATE:-/var/lib/apivo}"

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Logging: one JSON object per line, on stdout, for journald to capture.
#
# JSON rather than prose because this is the log an agent reads to answer
# "what happened to my deploy" without a shell on the box - the same reason
# the api emits JSON at APP_ENV=prod. `msg` is the only field that can carry
# arbitrary text, so it is the only one escaped.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
log() {
    _level="$1"
    _event="$2"
    _msg="$3"
    _msg=$(printf '%s' "$_msg" | sed -e 's/\\/\\\\/g' -e 's/"/\\"/g' | tr -d '\n\r\t')
    printf '{"level":"%s","event":"%s","env":"%s","msg":"%s"}\n' \
        "$_level" "$_event" "${ENV_NAME:-?}" "$_msg"
}

die() {
    log error "${1}" "${2}"
    # ::error:: as well as the JSON line: this script is also run by hand and
    # from CI, where the annotation is what a person actually sees.
    #
    # FLATTENED, because the message can now carry a subprocess's own output
    # - buildx's, on a failed resolve - and that output is multi-line. A
    # workflow command is line-oriented: a newline mid-message ends the
    # annotation early, spills the rest as loose log lines, and a line
    # beginning `::error::` inside that remainder would be an annotation
    # nobody wrote. Removing the newlines closes both at once.
    #
    # Newlines become SPACES rather than being deleted, unlike log(): that
    # writes a JSON string for tooling, where a lost space costs nothing,
    # while this line is read by a person and `read-only file systemERROR:`
    # is a worse sentence than the one buildx wrote.
    #
    # `::` itself is deliberately left alone. It is only a workflow command
    # at the START of a line, which the flattening already prevents, and
    # escaping it would corrupt any IPv6 address that appears in an error -
    # a registry failure is exactly where one shows up.
    _annotation=$(printf '%s' "${2}" | tr '\n\r\t' '   ')
    echo "::error::apivo-reconcile ${ENV_NAME:-?}: ${_annotation}" >&2
    exit "${3:-1}"
}

if [ "$#" -ne 1 ]; then
    echo "usage: $0 <env>" >&2
    exit 2
fi

ENV_NAME="$1"
# The environment name becomes container names, network names and file paths.
# It arrives from a systemd unit instance, which is user-supplied text, so it
# is validated rather than trusted: anything outside this set could escape a
# path or name a container in another environment.
case "$ENV_NAME" in
'' | *[!a-z0-9-]*)
    die usage "environment name '$ENV_NAME' is not lowercase alphanumeric with dashes" 2
    ;;
esac

ENV_DIR="$ETC/$ENV_NAME"
STATE_DIR="$STATE/$ENV_NAME"
STACK_ENV="$ENV_DIR/stack.env"

[ -r "$STACK_ENV" ] || die config "no readable $STACK_ENV; this host does not serve the '$ENV_NAME' environment (provision.sh creates it)" 2

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The maintenance switch. A reconciler with no way to stop it is a reconciler
# that fights an operator who is mid-investigation: `docker compose stop` on a
# broken container would be undone within the minute, along with the evidence.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
if [ -e "$ENV_DIR/paused" ]; then
    log info paused "reconciliation is paused by $ENV_DIR/paused; remove it to resume"
    exit 0
fi

# stack.env is structural configuration only - no application secrets - so
# sourcing it into this shell is deliberate and bounded. DATABASE_URL and the
# translation credential live in api.env, which the Docker daemon reads
# directly as the service's env_file and this script never opens.
set -a
# shellcheck source=/dev/null
. "$STACK_ENV"
set +a

# How long to wait for every container to report healthy before calling the
# rollout failed. The api migrates the schema on boot, so this is not just
# process start-up; a long migration on a large table is the case that makes
# a short timeout roll back a deploy that would have come up fine.
#
# Resolved AFTER stack.env is sourced, because stack.env is the only place
# docs/RELEASING.md tells an operator to set it and this unit has no
# EnvironmentFile. Read before the source, the value an operator wrote would
# be silently ignored and a long migration would be rolled back at 180s for
# reasons the journal never mentions.
WAIT_TIMEOUT="${APIVO_WAIT_TIMEOUT:-180}"

for _required in APIVO_ENV APIVO_CHANNEL APIVO_REGISTRY COMPOSE_FILE; do
    eval "_value=\${$_required:-}"
    [ -n "$_value" ] || die config "$STACK_ENV does not set $_required" 2
done

[ "$APIVO_ENV" = "$ENV_NAME" ] || die config "$STACK_ENV sets APIVO_ENV=$APIVO_ENV but this unit is '$ENV_NAME'; the two name the same environment or neither is trustworthy" 2
# The frontend's certificate, checked HERE rather than left to the container.
#
# compose sets SERVER_CERT_PATH and SERVER_KEY_PATH, which is what makes
# @astrojs/node serve https - and therefore what makes Astro.url carry the
# scheme the browser used, without which the site refuses its own form posts.
# Its standalone entry reads both files at startup with a plain readFileSync.
#
# Absent, that throws ENOENT and the container dies, restarts, and dies
# again. Nothing anywhere says why: a bind mount whose source is missing is
# CREATED EMPTY by Docker rather than refused, so the mount looks fine, the
# stack looks like it is merely unhealthy, and the actual sentence -
# "no such file or directory, open '/run/web-certs/web.crt'" - is buried in
# a restarting container's log.
#
# A host provisioned before this existed has no such file, so this is the
# state an upgrade lands in. It is worth one stat and a sentence that names
# the fix.
WEB_CERTS="$ENV_DIR/web-certs"
if [ ! -r "$WEB_CERTS/web.crt" ] || [ ! -r "$WEB_CERTS/web.key" ]; then
    die config "no frontend certificate at $WEB_CERTS; the web container would crash-loop on startup rather than serve. Re-run provision.sh on this host - it is idempotent and writes one per environment." 2
fi


API_REPO="$APIVO_REGISTRY/api"
WEB_REPO="$APIVO_REGISTRY/web"

mkdir -p "$STATE_DIR"
CURRENT="$STATE_DIR/current"
PREVIOUS="$STATE_DIR/previous"
IMAGES_ENV="$STATE_DIR/images.env"

# The digests the last successful rollout pinned, loaded before ANY compose
# invocation.
#
# This has to happen here rather than only inside the rollout, because the
# quiet path runs `compose up -d` too - that is what makes the reconciler
# self-healing - and the compose files declare
# `image: ${APIVO_API_IMAGE:?...}`. Without these in the environment, the most
# frequently executed path in the whole system fails on every tick with an
# unset variable, and reports a degraded environment that is in fact running
# perfectly well.
#
# Absent on a host that has never rolled out. That is not an error: the
# rollout below is what creates the file, and every path that runs compose
# before then sets these itself.
if [ -r "$IMAGES_ENV" ]; then
    set -a
    # shellcheck source=/dev/null
    . "$IMAGES_ENV"
    set +a
fi

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Resolve a tag to the digest the registry serves for it, WITHOUT pulling.
#
# `buildx imagetools inspect` is a registry query: on the overwhelmingly
# common tick - nothing has changed - this is two HTTP requests and no image
# data crosses the wire. Pulling first and comparing afterwards would work
# too, and would move gigabytes a day for an answer that is almost always
# "no".
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
resolve_digest() {
    # `{{println .Manifest.Digest}}`, NOT `{{.Manifest.Digest}}`.
    #
    # buildx ignores a --format that BEGINS with `{{.Manifest` and prints its
    # human-readable block instead - verified against buildx v0.31.1, the
    # version get.docker.com installs:
    #
    #   --format '{{.Manifest.Digest}}'         -> Name: ...\nMediaType: ...\nDigest: ...
    #   --format 'X{{.Manifest.Digest}}Y'       -> Xsha256:afa5c8...Y
    #   --format '{{println .Manifest.Digest}}' -> sha256:afa5c8...
    #
    # The trigger is purely the leading token, so the obvious form is the one
    # that silently does not work. It returns a multi-line block with exit 0,
    # which passes the emptiness check below, never matches a recorded digest,
    # and ends as `docker pull repo@Name:  ...` - rejected as an invalid
    # reference, reported as a registry failure, and no environment ever rolls
    # forward on any host.
    #
    # The error is KEPT, not sent to /dev/null. Discarding it cost an
    # afternoon on the first host ever provisioned: buildx said
    # `mkdir /root/.docker/buildx: read-only file system` and the operator
    # saw only "cannot resolve", whose three suggested causes were all wrong.
    # A `docker pull` by hand worked, which made the registry and the
    # credential look fine and left nothing to go on.
    #
    # It comes back on STDOUT, merged, rather than in a variable the caller
    # reads afterwards: this runs inside a command substitution, so a
    # variable set here dies with the subshell and the caller would print
    # nothing (or, under `set -u`, abort with a shell error instead of the
    # diagnosis). The exit status says which kind of output this is.
    $DOCKER buildx imagetools inspect "$1" --format '{{println .Manifest.Digest}}' 2>&1
}

# The one line of that output that is actually a digest.
#
# Anchored, so the human-readable block buildx prints when it ignores the
# --format (`Digest:    sha256:...`, with leading text) does NOT match and is
# correctly treated as "no digest". It also means a warning on stderr cannot
# be mistaken for the answer now that stderr is merged in.
digest_line() {
    printf '%s\n' "$1" | sed -n 's/^\(sha256:[0-9a-f][0-9a-f]*\)$/\1/p' | head -n 1
}

read_state_field() {
    # read_state_field <file> <key> - absent file or key yields empty, which
    # every caller treats as "nothing is recorded", never as an error.
    [ -r "$1" ] || return 0
    sed -n "s/^$2=//p" "$1" | head -n 1
}

compose() {
    # COMPOSE_FILE is exported from stack.env, so docker compose finds its own
    # files; the project name comes from the `name:` key in the base file.
    $DOCKER compose "$@"
}

# What the environment should be running, according to its channel. A failure
# reports buildx's own words rather than a guess at what went wrong.
if ! API_OUT=$(resolve_digest "$API_REPO:$APIVO_CHANNEL"); then
    die registry "cannot resolve $API_REPO:$APIVO_CHANNEL - $API_OUT. Nothing was changed; the environment keeps serving whatever it already had. If a plain 'docker pull' of that reference works by hand but this does not, the difference is the systemd sandbox this unit runs under, not the registry or the credential." 1
fi
if ! WEB_OUT=$(resolve_digest "$WEB_REPO:$APIVO_CHANNEL"); then
    die registry "cannot resolve $WEB_REPO:$APIVO_CHANNEL - $WEB_OUT. Nothing was changed; the environment keeps serving whatever it already had. If a plain 'docker pull' of that reference works by hand but this does not, the difference is the systemd sandbox this unit runs under, not the registry or the credential." 1
fi
API_DIGEST=$(digest_line "$API_OUT")
WEB_DIGEST=$(digest_line "$WEB_OUT")

if [ -z "$API_DIGEST" ] || [ -z "$WEB_DIGEST" ]; then
    die registry "cannot resolve $APIVO_REGISTRY/{api,web}:$APIVO_CHANNEL - buildx exited 0 but printed no digest, which is either a channel the publish workflow has never moved or the --format trap documented on resolve_digest. Nothing was changed; the environment keeps serving whatever it already had." 1
fi

RUNNING_API=$(read_state_field "$CURRENT" API_DIGEST)
RUNNING_WEB=$(read_state_field "$CURRENT" WEB_DIGEST)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The quiet path: the channel has not moved.
#
# `up -d` still runs, without --wait, and that is the self-healing property
# rather than a redundant call: a container that died, was OOM-killed, or was
# stopped by hand comes back on the next tick. It is a no-op when everything
# is already running, and it is the reason there is no separate "is anything
# down" alarm to write.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
if [ -n "$RUNNING_API" ] && [ "$API_DIGEST" = "$RUNNING_API" ] && [ "$WEB_DIGEST" = "$RUNNING_WEB" ]; then
    if compose up -d --remove-orphans >/dev/null 2>&1; then
        exit 0
    fi
    die converge "the channel has not moved, but bringing the existing stack up failed; the environment may be degraded. Check: docker compose ps" 1
fi

log info rollout_start "$APIVO_CHANNEL moved: api ${RUNNING_API:-none} -> $API_DIGEST, web ${RUNNING_WEB:-none} -> $WEB_DIGEST"

# The digests are pulled before anything is torn down, so a registry that
# fails half way costs nothing: the running stack is untouched until every
# byte of the new one is on the host.
if ! $DOCKER pull -q "$API_REPO@$API_DIGEST" >/dev/null 2>&1 || ! $DOCKER pull -q "$WEB_REPO@$WEB_DIGEST" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    die registry "failed to pull the pinned digests; the running stack was not touched" 1
fi

# The version the release pipeline stamped into the image, read from the
# image itself rather than from the tag that led here. This is what the
# frontend renders in its footer and what the release probe compares against,
# so it must come from the artefact.
image_version() {
    _v=$($DOCKER image inspect --format '{{index .Config.Labels "org.opencontainers.image.version"}}' "$1" 2>/dev/null || true)
    [ -n "$_v" ] || _v=dev
    printf '%s' "$_v"
}

IMAGE_VERSION=$(image_version "$API_REPO@$API_DIGEST")
WEB_VERSION=$(image_version "$WEB_REPO@$WEB_DIGEST")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The two channel tags do not move atomically.
#
# publish.yml points api:<channel> and web:<channel> at their digests in two
# separate registry calls, and this host may tick between them. Resolving the
# tags independently would then pin a NEW api beside the PREVIOUS web, roll it
# out, and report success - because the only version assertion downstream is
# against the api. A frontend a release behind its API is exactly the state
# that produces a blank page or a 500 on a field the old template does not
# know about.
#
# Refusing here costs nothing: the channel has not been consumed, so the next
# tick sixty seconds later sees the matched pair and rolls it out. The only
# way this becomes permanent is if the publish itself half-failed, which is a
# real problem that should be loud rather than silently deployed.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
if [ "$IMAGE_VERSION" != "$WEB_VERSION" ]; then
    log info version_skew "api is $IMAGE_VERSION but web is $WEB_VERSION; waiting for the channel to settle"
    exit 0
fi

write_images_env() {
    # write_images_env <api-digest> <web-digest> <version>
    # Written whole to a temporary file and renamed, so a compose run that
    # starts mid-write can never read half a pin. Same directory, so the
    # rename stays within one filesystem and cannot degrade to copy-then-
    # delete.
    _tmp="$IMAGES_ENV.new"
    {
        echo "# Written by apivo-reconcile. Hand edits are overwritten on the next tick."
        echo "APIVO_API_IMAGE=$API_REPO@$1"
        echo "APIVO_WEB_IMAGE=$WEB_REPO@$2"
        echo "APIVO_VERSION=$3"
    } > "$_tmp"
    mv "$_tmp" "$IMAGES_ENV"
    set -a
    # shellcheck source=/dev/null
    . "$IMAGES_ENV"
    set +a
}

record_state() {
    # record_state <file> <api-digest> <web-digest> <version>
    _tmp="$1.new"
    {
        echo "API_DIGEST=$2"
        echo "WEB_DIGEST=$3"
        echo "VERSION=$4"
        echo "AT=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)"
    } > "$_tmp"
    mv "$_tmp" "$1"
}

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Prove the roll-forward.
#
# `up -d --wait` returning 0 means every container reported HEALTHY, by its
# own healthcheck, which for the api means the binary answered its own
# /healthz. That is necessary and not sufficient: the PREVIOUS container
# answers a healthcheck just as happily if the new one never replaced it.
#
# So the containers are asked which image they are actually running, and it
# must be the digest just pinned. On Cloudflare this question could only be
# answered by trusting an HTTP response; here the daemon knows, so the
# stronger check is also the cheaper one.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
verify_running_digest() {
    # verify_running_digest <container> <expected-ref>
    _got=$($DOCKER container inspect --format '{{.Config.Image}}' "$1" 2>/dev/null || true)
    [ "$_got" = "$2" ] && return 0
    log error digest_mismatch "$1 is running '${_got:-nothing}', not the pinned '$2'"
    return 1
}

# And then, end to end: the frontend container fetches the api's /healthz
# across the compose network and reports the version the api SERVES. It
# proves the network path, the api's readiness and the version stamp in one
# request, and it needs no extra image on the host - the frontend runs Node,
# whose built-in fetch is what its own healthcheck already uses.
served_version() {
    $DOCKER exec "apivo-$ENV_NAME-web" node -e \
        'fetch("http://apivo-'"$ENV_NAME"'-api:8080/healthz").then(r=>r.json()).then(j=>process.stdout.write(String(j.version||""))).catch(()=>process.exit(1))' \
        2>/dev/null || true
}

roll_out() {
    # roll_out <api-digest> <web-digest> <version>
    write_images_env "$1" "$2" "$3"
    compose up -d --remove-orphans --wait --wait-timeout "$WAIT_TIMEOUT" || return 1
    verify_running_digest "apivo-$ENV_NAME-api" "$API_REPO@$1" || return 1
    verify_running_digest "apivo-$ENV_NAME-web" "$WEB_REPO@$2" || return 1

    _served=$(served_version)
    if [ "$_served" != "$3" ]; then
        log error version_mismatch "the api serves version '${_served:-no answer}', expected '$3'"
        return 1
    fi
    return 0
}

if roll_out "$API_DIGEST" "$WEB_DIGEST" "$IMAGE_VERSION"; then
    # The state that was good is kept as the rollback target only AFTER the
    # new one is proven, so `previous` always names a rollout that once
    # served rather than merely one that was attempted.
    [ -r "$CURRENT" ] && cp "$CURRENT" "$PREVIOUS"
    record_state "$CURRENT" "$API_DIGEST" "$WEB_DIGEST" "$IMAGE_VERSION"

    # Yesterday's images are the other way a small host fills its disk.
    #
    # The age filter is load-bearing, not caution. Every image here is pulled
    # BY DIGEST, so none of them carries a tag - and an untagged image is
    # what `docker image prune` calls dangling and removes by default. The
    # release this host would roll back to is untagged and, once the new one
    # is serving, referenced by no container: a bare prune is entitled to
    # delete the very thing `previous` names. `apivoctl rollback` would then
    # depend on re-pulling from a registry that may be exactly what is
    # unavailable when someone is breaking glass.
    #
    # `until` keeps anything pulled in the last week, which covers every
    # rollback target worth having while still bounding the disk.
    $DOCKER image prune -f --filter "until=${APIVO_IMAGE_RETENTION:-168h}" >/dev/null 2>&1 || true

    log info rollout_ok "$ENV_NAME now serves $IMAGE_VERSION (api $API_DIGEST)"
    exit 0
fi

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The rollout failed. Put back what was serving.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
log error rollout_failed "rolling back $ENV_NAME to the previous digest"

PREV_API=$(read_state_field "$CURRENT" API_DIGEST)
PREV_WEB=$(read_state_field "$CURRENT" WEB_DIGEST)
PREV_VERSION=$(read_state_field "$CURRENT" VERSION)

if [ -z "$PREV_API" ]; then
    die rollback_impossible "the rollout failed and there is no previous digest to return to - this environment has never had a successful one. It is DOWN. The channel still points at the broken build, so every tick will retry it: pause with 'touch $ENV_DIR/paused' before investigating, and check 'docker compose logs'." 1
fi

if roll_out "$PREV_API" "$PREV_WEB" "${PREV_VERSION:-dev}"; then
    die rolled_back "the rollout failed and $ENV_NAME was rolled back to ${PREV_VERSION:-the previous digest}. The channel still points at the broken build, so the next tick will try it again - fix it forward, or move the channel back." 1
fi

die rollback_failed "the rollout failed AND the rollback to ${PREV_VERSION:-the previous digest} also failed. $ENV_NAME is DOWN and no automatic path remains: pause with 'touch $ENV_DIR/paused', then investigate with 'docker compose ps' and 'docker compose logs'." 1

1	# The runtime, for every environment.
2	#
3	# ONE file serves qa, staging and production. The environment is a variable,
4	# not a fork: `APIVO_ENV` names it, and everything that differs between
5	# environments differs in the env files under /etc/apivo/<env>/ — never
6	# here. That is deliberate. Three near-identical compose files drift the
7	# moment one of them is edited in a hurry, and the whole point of a staging
8	# environment is that it is shaped like production. Parity by construction
9	# beats parity by discipline.
10	#
11	# What genuinely differs between environments:
12	#
13	#   qa       a Postgres container on this host (docker-compose.local-db.yml
14	#            is layered on via COMPOSE_FILE), throwaway data
15	#   staging  its own Supabase EU project, production-shaped
16	#   prod     its own Supabase EU project, on its own VPS
17	#
18	# All three run APP_ENV=prod. That is not a mistake: `prod` in this codebase
19	# means "hardened" — JSON logs, Secure cookies, a DATABASE_URL that must be
20	# encrypted — not "the production instance". A QA environment that runs with
21	# the guards off is a QA environment that cannot find the bugs the guards
22	# would have caught.
23	#
24	# Images are ALWAYS pinned by digest. The reconciler
25	# (deploy/hetzner/bin/apivo-reconcile) resolves the environment's channel
26	# tag to a digest and writes it to /var/lib/apivo/<env>/images.env, which is
27	# where ${APIVO_API_IMAGE} and ${APIVO_WEB_IMAGE} below come from. A tag is
28	# what an environment *tracks*; a digest is what it *runs*.
29	
30	name: apivo-${APIVO_ENV}
31	
32	services:
33	  # The Go API. Not published on any host port and not reachable from the
34	  # edge network's outside — Caddy is the only thing that talks to it, over
35	  # the compose network by container name. Same topology as every other
36	  # deployment this project has had (specs/001-epiloyes-alpha/contracts):
37	  # the API is not publicly routable, in any environment.
38	  api:
39	    image: ${APIVO_API_IMAGE:?the reconciler must pin an api image digest}
40	    container_name: apivo-${APIVO_ENV}-api
41	    restart: unless-stopped
42	    # Secrets live in this file and are read by the Docker daemon, not by
43	    # the reconciler: `env_file` keeps DATABASE_URL out of the reconciler's
44	    # process environment and out of `docker compose config` output.
45	    env_file:
46	      - ${APIVO_ETC:-/etc/apivo}/${APIVO_ENV}/api.env
47	    environment:
48	      HTTP_ADDR: ":8080"
49	      # Hardened everywhere. See the note at the top of this file.
50	      APP_ENV: prod
51	    networks:
52	      - edge
53	      - data
54	    # A VPS has a finite disk and no platform sweeping logs away. Unbounded
55	    # json-file logging is the single most common way a small host runs out
56	    # of space, and it takes the whole box down with it, every environment
57	    # on it at once.
58	    logging:
59	      driver: json-file
60	      options:
61	        max-size: ${APIVO_LOG_MAX_SIZE:-10m}
62	        max-file: ${APIVO_LOG_MAX_FILE:-3}
63	    # The image declares its own HEALTHCHECK (the binary probes itself), so
64	    # nothing is restated here. `docker compose up -d --wait` honours it,
65	    # which is what makes the reconciler's rollout gate real.
66	    deploy:
67	      resources:
68	        limits:
69	          cpus: ${APIVO_API_CPUS:-1.0}
70	          memory: ${APIVO_API_MEMORY:-512M}
71	    security_opt:
72	      - no-new-privileges:true
73	
74	  # The Astro frontend. Also unpublished: Caddy fronts it.
75	  web:
76	    image: ${APIVO_WEB_IMAGE:?the reconciler must pin a web image digest}
77	    container_name: apivo-${APIVO_ENV}-web
78	    restart: unless-stopped
79	    env_file:
80	      - ${APIVO_ETC:-/etc/apivo}/${APIVO_ENV}/web.env
81	    environment:
82	      HOST: 0.0.0.0
83	      PORT: "4321"
84	      # The frontend renders every page server-side from the API. On this
85	      # deployment that is a private hop across the compose network by
86	      # container name — no exit to the public internet and back, which is
87	      # what the Cloudflare Containers shape forced (a container there is
88	      # reachable only through its Durable Object, so the deployment's own
89	      # public origin was the only address the web container had). Worth
90	      # naming as a straight win of moving to a VPS.
91	      API_BASE_URL: http://apivo-${APIVO_ENV}-api:8080
92	      # Rendered in the footer's fine print, and the thing the release probe
